title: Beads from Shiva's tears
hook: Shiva opens his eyes after a long meditation, and his tears become the seeds of a mala
carry: all things strung on God, like mala beads

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna said the mind is like the wind, and Krishna agreed: practice and letting go hold the restless mind.

In the Shiva Purana, Shiva sits in meditation for a thousand years of the gods. When at last he opens his eyes, tears fall from them to the earth. Where they land, trees grow, and their seeds are called rudraksha: Rudra's eye, Rudra being a name of Shiva. Dark, knobbly seeds, with lines running down their sides. Devotees of Shiva string them into a mala, and many wear one, or count a mantra on it, every day.
screen: `SHIVA OPENS HIS EYES.` → `HIS TEARS FALL.` → `THEY GROW INTO RUDRAKSHA.`

segments.voice: Mala means a garland, the same word as flowers placed around a neck or on an image of God. A japa mala is a garland for counting a mantra. Devotees of Shiva favor rudraksha; devotees of Vishnu and Krishna favor tulsi wood, from the holy basil many families tend at home. One bead is larger and sits apart, with a tassel: the meru, sharing its name with the sacred mountain at the center of the world. Teachers in several lineages say not to cross it; at the end of a round, you turn the string and go back. Their reasons vary. Some say the meru stands for the guru or for God, and you don't step over what you honor. Others say turning back keeps each round awake. Now the teaching the beads carry. In the Gita's seventh chapter, Krishna says all of this world is strung on him, like gems on a thread. The beads are what you see; the thread holding them is hidden. That's a central Hindu teaching: the many things of the world aren't scattered. One divine reality runs through them all, the way one cord runs through every bead. And in the sixth chapter Krishna says, wherever the restless mind wanders, bring it back. The bead is that return, made into something your thumb can feel. The mind drifts to a bill or a text; the thumb moves to the next bead; you're back on the thread. Shiva's seeds or Vishnu's basil, the mala teaches with your hands: many beads, one thread.
screen: `MALA: A GARLAND FOR COUNTING.` · `THE MERU: THE BEAD YOU DON'T CROSS.` · `ALL STRUNG ON ONE THREAD.` · `EACH BEAD, A RETURN TO THE THREAD.`

segments.voice: Hold a mala if you have one, or touch the thumb to each fingertip in turn, saying your mantra once with each touch, silently or in a whisper; Om will do, or a word from your own tradition. When the mind drifts, don't scold it; let the next touch be the coming back. At the end of a round, pause, turn around, and go back the other way.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, the tool in the hand: the mala, its meru, and the one thread running through every bead.
Hold on to it: all things strung on God, like mala beads. Each bead brings you back to the thread. Same time tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1013 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NARADA ASKS FOR THE RULES.`

howItsDone: Hindus who keep japa may count on a mala, a string of beads of tulsi wood, rudraksha or other materials, moving one bead per repetition and turning the string at the larger meru bead rather than crossing it.
